title: The Multiplication Principle: counting without listing

board_content.text: How do we count a HUGE collection without listing it?
Thali counter: pick 1 sabzi (4 options), 1 roti (3), 1 sweet (2).
For every sabzi all 3 rotis stay open; for every pair both sweets stay open. Choices STACK by multiplying.

board_content.text: AND (this and then that) means multiply.
A 6-character password from letters and digits has over two billion settings. No one lists that.

segments_english.text: <curious>How do you count something enormous without ever writing out the list? That single question is what this whole chapter answers, and it starts from one clean idea.
Picture a small thali counter near a railway station. You pick one sabzi from four, one roti from three, one sweet from two. The owner says many plates are possible, and we want the exact number.

Here is the key move. Whatever sabzi you take, all three rotis are still open; and for every sabzi and roti pair, both sweets are still there. So the counts do not add, they stack up by multiplying: four times three times two, which is twenty four distinct thalis.
That stacking is the Multiplication Principle, the heart of the Fundamental Principle of Counting. When you make a sequence of independent choices, you multiply the number of options at each stage.

See it as a tree growing left to right. Four branches for the sabzis, each splitting into three for the rotis, each splitting again into two for the sweets. The leaves on the far right are the complete thalis, and counting leaves is just multiplying the branching numbers.
The trigger word is AND. Sabzi and roti and sweet, do this and then that, means the choices combine, and combining means multiply.

Why not just list everything? Because lists explode. A six character password built from letters and digits has over two billion settings. The genius here is that you get the size of the collection while staying blissfully ignorant of its members.

segments_hinglish.text: <curious>इतनी बड़ी चीज़ को बिना list बनाए कैसे count करें? यही सवाल इस पूरे chapter की जान है, और शुरुआत होती है एक clean idea से।
Railway station के पास वाला एक छोटा thali counter सोचो। आप एक sabzi चार में से चुनते हो, एक roti तीन में से, एक sweet दो में से। Owner कहता है बहुत plates possible हैं, और हमें exact number चाहिए।

Key move यह है। कोई भी sabzi लो, तीनों rotis अभी भी open हैं; और हर sabzi और roti pair के लिए दोनों sweets भी। तो counts add नहीं होते, वो multiply होकर stack होते हैं: four into three into two, यानी twenty four अलग thalis।
यही stacking है Multiplication Principle, जो Fundamental Principle of Counting का दिल है। जब आप independent choices की एक sequence बनाते हो, तो हर stage के options को multiply करते हो।

इसे एक tree की तरह देखो जो left से right बढ़ रहा है। Sabzis के लिए चार branches, हर एक rotis के लिए तीन में बँटती है, फिर हर एक sweets के लिए दो में। दाईं तरफ के leaves ही पूरी thalis हैं, और leaves गिनना बस branching numbers को multiply करना है।
Trigger word है AND। Sabzi और roti और sweet, ये करो फिर वो, मतलब choices combine होती हैं, और combine का मतलब multiply।

सब कुछ list क्यों न करें? क्योंकि lists explode कर जाती हैं। Letters और digits से बना छह character का password two billion से ज़्यादा settings रखता है। यहाँ का genius यह है कि collection का size मिल जाता है जबकि आप उसके members से पूरी तरह अनजान रहते हो।

title: The Addition Principle: AND vs OR

board_content.text: What if you choose ONE pile OR the other, not both?
Offer: take one of 4 sabzis OR one of 2 sweets, but not both.
OR (this or instead that), mutually exclusive, means add.
AND combines choices, so multiply. OR gives alternatives, so add.
Addition needs mutually exclusive options. If the piles overlap, naive adding double-counts.
Burn it in: AND multiplies, OR adds.

segments_english.text: Now change the story a little. The owner says: today take either one of four sabzis or one of two sweets, but not both. This is a completely different situation from before.
You are no longer building a plate stage by stage. You make a single choice from one pile or from the other, and the two piles do not mix.
So you do not multiply here, you add: four sabzi options or two sweet options give four plus two, which is six ways in total. This is the Addition Principle.
The signal word has changed from AND to OR. OR means alternatives, one route instead of the other, and alternatives are added together.
So the whole distinction lives in two tiny English words. AND, do this and then that, combines the choices, so you multiply. OR, do this or instead that, gives alternatives, so you add.

One warning that examiners love. Addition only works when the options are mutually exclusive, with no overlap. If the two piles share a member, naive adding counts it twice, and you must subtract the overlap back later.
So before touching any numbers, translate the problem into ANDs and ORs. That single reading decides whether you reach for multiply or for add.

segments_hinglish.text: अब story थोड़ी बदलो। Owner कहता है: आज या तो चार sabzis में से एक लो, या दो sweets में से एक, but दोनों नहीं। यह पहले से बिल्कुल अलग situation है।
अब आप stage by stage plate नहीं बना रहे। आप एक ही choice करते हो, एक pile से या दूसरे से, और दोनों piles आपस में mix नहीं होतीं।
तो यहाँ multiply नहीं करते, add करते हो: चार sabzi options या दो sweet options मिलकर four plus two, यानी total छह ways। यही है Addition Principle।
Signal word AND से बदलकर OR हो गया। OR का मतलब alternatives, एक रास्ता दूसरे की जगह, और alternatives को add किया जाता है।
तो पूरा फ़र्क़ दो छोटे English words में है। AND, ये करो फिर वो, choices combine करता है, इसलिए multiply। OR, ये करो या उसकी जगह वो, alternatives देता है, इसलिए add।
एक warning जो examiners को बहुत पसंद है। Addition तभी काम करता है जब options mutually exclusive हों, कोई overlap न हो। अगर दोनों piles में कोई common member है, तो naive adding उसे दो बार गिन लेगा।
तो numbers छूने से पहले, problem को ANDs और ORs में translate करो। यही एक reading तय करती है कि multiply करना है या add।

title: Factorial: the whole arrangement in one symbol

board_content.text: Arrange 5 different trophies in a row. How many orders?
A descending product of naturals is so common it earns a shorthand.
$0! = 1$, never 0 (justified next).
Defined only for non-negative integers: not negatives, not fractions.

segments_english.text: Where does the factorial come from? Suppose you line up five different trophies on a shelf, and you want to know how many orders are possible.

The first position can be filled by any of the five trophies; the next by any of the remaining four; then three; then two; then the last one. This is a pure multiplication principle chain: five times four times three times two times one, which is one hundred twenty.
That descending product of natural numbers turns up so often that mathematicians gave it a shorthand.
We write it as five factorial, with an exclamation mark, and it equals one hundred twenty. So a factorial is simply the multiplication principle applied to a full arrangement.
In general, n factorial is n times n minus one, times n minus two, all the way down to one. Keep the meaning in your head, not just the symbol: it counts the orders of n distinct things.
<whisper>Here is a definition that surprises everyone: zero factorial equals one, not zero. We will justify that properly in a moment, so do not just memorise it.
And a boundary rule: factorial is defined only for non-negative integers. You cannot take the factorial of a negative number or a fraction at this level.

segments_hinglish.text: Factorial आता कहाँ से है? मान लो आप एक shelf पर पाँच अलग trophies लगाते हो, और जानना चाहते हो कितने orders possible हैं।

पहली position कोई भी पाँच में से भर सकती है; अगली बची हुई चार में से; फिर तीन; फिर दो; फिर आख़िरी एक। यह pure multiplication principle chain है: five into four into three into two into one, यानी one hundred twenty।
Natural numbers का यह descending product इतनी बार आता है कि mathematicians ने इसे एक shorthand दे दिया।
इसे हम five factorial लिखते हैं, exclamation mark के साथ, और यह बराबर है one hundred twenty। तो factorial बस multiplication principle है जो एक पूरे arrangement पर लगा है।
General में, n factorial मतलब n into n minus one, into n minus two, नीचे one तक। Symbol नहीं, meaning याद रखो: यह n distinct चीज़ों के orders गिनता है।
<whisper>एक definition जो सबको चौंकाती है: zero factorial equals one, zero नहीं। इसे हम अभी properly justify करेंगे, तो बस रट मत लेना।
और एक boundary rule: factorial सिर्फ़ non-negative integers के लिए defined है। इस level पर आप negative number या fraction का factorial नहीं ले सकते।

title: Core formulas: multiply, add, factorial, and the repetition fork

board_content.text: Your foundation toolkit
3 structures: repetition $\to n^r$; no repeat, order matters $\to$ falling product; arrange all $\to n!$
Factorials explode: $5!=120$ but $10!=3{,}628{,}800$. Leave a huge answer as, say, $20!$.

segments_english.text: Let me put your foundation formulas on one board, so you can reach for the right one instantly.
First, the multiplication principle for a chain of stages: m one times m two, up to m k. This is the AND situation, where every stage combines with the next.
Second, the addition principle: m plus n. This is the OR situation, for mutually exclusive alternatives.
Third, the factorial: n factorial is n times n minus one, down to one, with zero factorial defined as one.
Fourth, and this is the identity you will use most, the recursion: n factorial equals n times n minus one factorial. It lets you peel off one factor at a time.
Fifth, counting with repetition. If r slots are each filled independently from the same n options, the count is n to the power r, because every slot sees the full n options afresh.

Keep three structures straight, because the whole chapter forks between them. Repetition allowed gives n to the r. No repetition with order gives a falling product. Arranging all n distinct objects gives n factorial.

One sanity habit: factorials grow ferociously. Five factorial is only one hundred twenty, but ten factorial is over three point six million. So if an exam answer comes out as, say, twenty factorial, you leave it as twenty factorial rather than computing it.

segments_hinglish.text: अपने foundation formulas एक ही board पर रख देता हूँ, ताकि आप सही वाला instantly पकड़ सको।
पहला, stages की chain के लिए multiplication principle: m one into m two, m k तक। यह AND situation है, जहाँ हर stage अगले के साथ combine होती है।
दूसरा, addition principle: m plus n। यह OR situation है, mutually exclusive alternatives के लिए।
तीसरा, factorial: n factorial मतलब n into n minus one, नीचे one तक, और zero factorial को one define किया गया है।
चौथा, और यही identity आप सबसे ज़्यादा use करोगे, recursion: n factorial equals n into n minus one factorial। यह एक-एक factor छीलने देती है।
पाँचवाँ, repetition के साथ counting। अगर r slots हर एक same n options में से independently भरे जाएँ, तो count होता है n to the power r, क्योंकि हर slot को पूरे n options फिर से दिखते हैं।

तीन structures साफ़ रखो, क्योंकि पूरा chapter इन्हीं के बीच fork करता है। Repetition allowed देता है n to the r। No repetition with order देता है falling product। सारे n distinct objects arrange करना देता है n factorial।

एक sanity habit: factorials बहुत तेज़ी से बढ़ते हैं। Five factorial सिर्फ़ one hundred twenty है, पर ten factorial three point six million से ऊपर। तो अगर answer twenty factorial आए, उसे twenty factorial ही छोड़ दो, compute मत करो।

title: Proof: box-filling, and how it builds the factorial

board_content.text: Why the multiplication principle is TRUE (not magic)

board_content.svg: <svg font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" viewBox="0 0 420 200" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><text x="55" y="48" font-size="12" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif">Box 1: m ways</text><rect x="45" y="58" width="80" height="80" fill="none" stroke="#333" stroke-width="2"/><text x="255" y="22" font-size="12" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif">Box 2: n ways (each)</text><rect x="255" y="30" width="110" height="140" fill="none" stroke="#333" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="85" cy="80" r="4" fill="#c8102e"/><circle cx="85" cy="98" r="4" fill="#333"/><circle cx="85" cy="116" r="4" fill="#333"/><line x1="89" y1="80" x2="255" y2="55" stroke="#999"/><line x1="89" y1="80" x2="255" y2="85" stroke="#999"/><line x1="89" y1="80" x2="255" y2="115" stroke="#999"/><line x1="89" y1="80" x2="255" y2="145" stroke="#999"/><circle cx="310" cy="55" r="3" fill="#333"/><circle cx="310" cy="85" r="3" fill="#333"/><circle cx="310" cy="115" r="3" fill="#333"/><circle cx="310" cy="145" r="3" fill="#333"/><text x="60" y="190" font-size="12" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif">each of m choices reaches all n → m × n outcomes</text></svg>
board_content.caption: Each Box-1 choice fans into all n Box-2 options

board_content.text: Box 1 fills in $m$ ways. Fix one. Box 2 still fills in $n$ ways, the SAME $n$ whichever Box-1 option you fixed.

board_content.latex: m \text{ groups} \times n \text{ each} = m \times n

board_content.text: Fine print: Box 2's count must not depend on Box 1's choice (independence).
Same idea derives $n!$: positions take $n, n-1, \dots, 1$ objects, product is $n!$.
And $0!=1$: recursion $1! = 1\cdot 0!$ forces it, and there is exactly one way to arrange nothing.

segments_english.text: The multiplication principle is not a theorem pulled from thin air, and an examiner rewards you for justifying it. So let us see exactly why it is true.
Think of the task as filling two boxes, left to right, and watch how the choices fan out.
Box one can be filled in m ways. Now fix any one of those choices. With that locked, box two can still be filled in n ways, and crucially this n is the same no matter which box one option you fixed.

So each of the m box-one choices spawns exactly n complete outcomes. Grouping the outcomes by their box-one choice gives m groups of n each, which is m times n, with none missed and none double-counted.
The fine print is that independence assumption: box two's count must not depend on which option box one used. Hold onto that, because it is exactly where harder problems set traps.

The same box-filling argument derives the factorial. Treat the n positions as n boxes: position one takes any of n objects, position two any of the remaining n minus one, and so on down to one. Multiply, and you get n factorial.

It even pins down zero factorial. The recursion says one factorial equals one times zero factorial, which forces zero factorial to be one. And by meaning, there is exactly one way to arrange nothing, the empty arrangement.

segments_hinglish.text: Multiplication principle हवा से निकाला हुआ theorem नहीं है, और examiner आपको इसे justify करने के marks देता है। तो देखते हैं यह true क्यों है।
Task को दो boxes भरने की तरह सोचो, left से right, और देखो choices कैसे fan out होती हैं।
Box one m ways में भर सकता है। अब कोई एक choice fix करो। उसे lock करके, box two अभी भी n ways में भर सकता है, और important बात, यह n same रहता है चाहे आपने box one का कोई भी option fix किया हो।
तो m box-one choices में से हर एक ठीक n complete outcomes पैदा करती है। Outcomes को उनके box-one choice से group करो तो m groups मिलते हैं, हर एक में n, यानी m into n, न कोई छूटा न कोई double गिना।
Fine print वही independence assumption है: box two का count इस पर depend नहीं करना चाहिए कि box one ने कौन सा option लिया। इसे पकड़े रखो, क्योंकि यहीं harder problems traps लगाती हैं।

यही box-filling argument factorial भी derive करता है। n positions को n boxes समझो: position one कोई भी n objects लेता है, position two बची n minus one में से, और नीचे one तक। Multiply करो, मिलता है n factorial।

यह zero factorial भी pin कर देता है। Recursion कहती है one factorial equals one into zero factorial, जो zero factorial को one होने पर मजबूर करती है। और meaning से, कुछ भी न arrange करने का ठीक एक तरीका है, empty arrangement।

title: When independence breaks: reorder or split into cases

board_content.text: The trap: a later stage depends on an earlier choice
Form 3-digit numbers, all digits distinct, from {0,1,2,3}. No leading zero.
Reflex $4\times3\times2=24$ is WRONG: slot 1 can't use 0.
Fix the constrained slot FIRST: slot 1 in 3 ways (digits 1, 2, 3).
Now slots 2 and 3 draw from the 3 remaining digits, which now include 0.
Rule: reorder so the constrained stage is first, or split into cases and add.

segments_english.text: The multiplication principle has one piece of fine print, and Advanced problems live in the gap when it fails. Let me show it breaking.
Form three-digit numbers with all digits distinct, using the set zero, one, two, three, and no leading zero is allowed.
The reflex answer, four times three times two equals twenty four, is wrong. The first slot cannot use zero, so its count is not the same as the later slots, and the clean symmetry is gone.
The fix is to handle the constrained slot first. Slot one can be one, two, or three, so it has three ways, not four.
Once slot one is chosen, slots two and three draw from the three remaining digits, and those now include zero because the leading rule no longer applies here.
So the count is three, times three times two, which is three times six, giving eighteen, not twenty four.

The general lesson: when a stage's options depend on an earlier choice, either reorder so the constrained stage comes first, or split the problem into disjoint cases and add them. Casework plus the counting principle together handle essentially every problem you will meet.

segments_hinglish.text: Multiplication principle में एक fine print है, और Advanced problems उसी gap में रहती हैं जब वो fail होती है। दिखाता हूँ इसे टूटते हुए।
तीन-digit numbers बनाओ जिनके सारे digits distinct हों, set zero, one, two, three से, और leading zero allowed नहीं है।
Reflex answer, four into three into two equals twenty four, ग़लत है। पहला slot zero use नहीं कर सकता, तो उसका count बाद वाले slots जैसा नहीं है, और clean symmetry ख़त्म हो गई।
Fix यह है कि constrained slot पहले handle करो। Slot one one, two, या three हो सकता है, तो इसके तीन ways हैं, चार नहीं।
Slot one चुनने के बाद, slots two और three बची तीन digits में से लेते हैं, और उनमें अब zero भी है क्योंकि leading rule यहाँ लागू नहीं होती।
तो count है three, into three into two, यानी three into six, जो देता है eighteen, twenty four नहीं।

General lesson: जब किसी stage के options पहले की choice पर depend करें, या तो reorder करो ताकि constrained stage पहले आए, या problem को disjoint cases में तोड़कर add करो। Casework और counting principle मिलकर लगभग हर problem संभाल लेते हैं।

title: Worked examples: clean multiplication and the AND/OR mix

board_content.text: Example 1 (CBSE): ID codes
Code = one letter (A-Z) then three digits (0-9), digit repetition allowed.
Example 2: breakfast order (AND vs OR)
Either one ready plate (3) OR a combo of one paratha (4) AND one chutney (5).
Bracket each AND-group with $\times$, then join alternatives with $+$.

segments_english.text: Let us cash out the theory on two clean examples. First, a CBSE-level one about ID codes.
A school issues codes made of one letter from A to Z, followed by three digits from zero to nine, and digit repetition is allowed. We fill four slots in order.

The letter slot has twenty six ways; each of the three digit slots has ten ways. By the counting principle we multiply: twenty six times ten times ten times ten, which is twenty six thousand codes. Notice the clean rhythm: identify slots, count each, multiply, state the answer.
The second example mixes AND and OR, which is exactly the trap this chapter is built to catch.
A canteen lets you either take a single ready plate, of which there are three, or build a combo of one paratha from four types and one chutney from five types.

The combo is paratha and chutney, an AND, so we multiply to get four times five, which is twenty. The overall order is ready plate or combo, mutually exclusive, so we add: three plus twenty, giving twenty three ways.

A panicking student multiplies everything to get sixty, or adds everything to get twelve. Both ignore the AND-OR structure. The mechanical fix is to bracket each AND group with a times sign, then join the independent alternatives with a plus.

segments_hinglish.text: Theory को दो clean examples पर cash out करते हैं। पहला, CBSE-level, ID codes का।
एक school codes issue करता है जो एक letter A से Z, फिर तीन digits zero से nine से बनते हैं, और digit repetition allowed है। हम चार slots order में भरते हैं।

Letter slot के twenty six ways; तीनों digit slots हर एक के ten ways। Counting principle से multiply: twenty six into ten into ten into ten, यानी twenty six thousand codes। इस rhythm पर ध्यान दो: slots पहचानो, हर एक count करो, multiply करो, answer बोलो।
दूसरा example AND और OR mix करता है, यही वो trap है जिसके लिए यह chapter बना है।
एक canteen आपको या तो एक ready plate देता है, जो तीन हैं, या एक combo बनाने देता है, एक paratha चार types में से और एक chutney पाँच types में से।
Combo है paratha और chutney, एक AND, तो multiply करके four into five, यानी twenty। Overall order है ready plate या combo, mutually exclusive, तो add: three plus twenty, यानी twenty three ways।

घबराया हुआ student सब multiply करके sixty निकालता है, या सब add करके twelve। दोनों AND-OR structure ignore करते हैं। Mechanical fix: हर AND group को times sign से bracket करो, फिर independent alternatives को plus से जोड़ो।

title: Worked examples: constrained slots and complementary counting

board_content.text: Example 3 (JEE Main): even 4-digit numbers, repetition allowed
Handle constrained slots first: thousands $\ne 0$; units must be even.
Example 4 (JEE Adv): 5-digit numbers with at least one 9
"At least one" $\to$ count the complement.

segments_english.text: Now two harder examples, both about digit constraints. The reflex to build here is: handle the most constrained slot first.
Example three asks how many four-digit numbers are even, with digit repetition allowed. Two constraints bite at once: the thousands place cannot be zero, and the units place must be even.

So the thousands place has nine ways, from one to nine; the units place has five ways, from zero, two, four, six, eight; and the hundreds and tens each have all ten digits. These are independent, so multiply: nine times ten times ten times five, which gives four thousand five hundred even numbers.
Example four is JEE Advanced. How many five-digit numbers contain the digit nine at least once, no leading zero, repetition allowed?

Counting at least one nine directly means adding the cases of exactly one, two, three, four, or five nines, watching for overcounting. The clean route is the complement: all five-digit numbers minus those with no nine at all.

All five-digit numbers: first digit from one to nine is nine ways, the other four from zero to nine is ten each, giving ninety thousand. Numbers with no nine: the first digit drops both zero and nine, leaving eight ways; each other digit drops only nine, leaving nine ways, giving eight times nine to the fourth, which is fifty two thousand four hundred eighty eight.

<whisper>Here is the subtle point that Advanced loves. The leading digit obeys two exclusions at once, not zero and not nine, so it has eight, while interior digits obey only one and have nine. Subtracting gives ninety thousand minus fifty two thousand four hundred eighty eight, which is thirty seven thousand five hundred twelve.

segments_hinglish.text: अब दो harder examples, दोनों digit constraints के बारे में। यहाँ जो reflex बनाना है: सबसे constrained slot पहले handle करो।
Example three पूछता है कितने four-digit numbers even हैं, digit repetition allowed। दो constraints एक साथ लगती हैं: thousands place zero नहीं हो सकता, और units place even होना चाहिए।

तो thousands place के nine ways, one से nine; units place के five ways, zero, two, four, six, eight में से; और hundreds और tens हर एक के सारे ten digits। ये independent हैं, तो multiply: nine into ten into ten into five, जो देता है four thousand five hundred even numbers।
Example four JEE Advanced है। कितने five-digit numbers में digit nine at least once आता है, leading zero नहीं, repetition allowed?

At least one nine को directly count करना मतलब exactly one, two, three, four, या five nines के cases add करना, overcounting से बचते हुए। Clean route है complement: सारे five-digit numbers minus वो जिनमें कोई nine नहीं।

सारे five-digit numbers: first digit one से nine, nine ways, बाकी चार zero से nine, ten-ten, यानी ninety thousand। बिना nine वाले: first digit zero और nine दोनों drop करता है, बचते हैं eight ways; हर बाकी digit सिर्फ़ nine drop करता है, बचते हैं nine ways, यानी eight into nine to the fourth, जो है fifty two thousand four hundred eighty eight।

<whisper>यहाँ वो subtle point है जो Advanced को पसंद है। Leading digit दो exclusions एक साथ मानता है, न zero न nine, तो उसके eight; जबकि interior digits सिर्फ़ एक मानते हैं और उनके nine। घटाओ तो ninety thousand minus fifty two thousand four hundred eighty eight, यानी thirty seven thousand five hundred twelve।

title: Pitfalls & pro-tips: AND/OR, the repetition fork, and 0!

board_content.text: The mistakes that cost marks here
Confusing AND with OR. Translate to AND/OR first, THEN assign $\times$ or $+$.
Assuming 'no repetition' by default. Locks, plates, passwords usually allow it: $n^r$.
Leading digit can face two exclusions at once ($\ne 0$ and $\ne 9 \to 8$, not 9).
Treating $0!$ as 0. It is 1, or later combination formulas collapse.
Adding overlapping OR-cases. Mutually exclusive only, else you double-count the overlap.
Pro-tip: 'at least one' $\to$ Total $-$ none.

segments_english.text: Let me close the subtopic with the mistakes that quietly cost marks, so you can spot them in yourself.

The most frequent error is confusing AND with OR: multiplying mutually exclusive alternatives, or adding sequential stages. Always translate the words into ANDs and ORs first, and only then assign a times or a plus.

The second is assuming no repetition by default. Many students reflexively write falling products. But locks, number plates, and passwords usually allow repetition, which is n to the r, not a falling product. That fork decides everything.

Third, forgetting boundary constraints. In digit problems the leading digit usually cannot be zero, and it can face two exclusions at once, such as not zero and not nine, which leaves eight options, not nine. Slot the most constrained position first.
Fourth, mishandling zero factorial. It is one, never zero. Treating it as zero collapses the combination formulas you will meet soon into nonsense.

Fifth, adding overlapping OR-cases. The addition principle needs the cases to be mutually exclusive. If your two piles share members, naive addition double-counts, and you must subtract the overlap back.

<whisper>And the pro-tip worth gold: whenever you see the words 'at least one', do not grind through casework. Compute total minus none. It turns a messy sum into two clean products almost every time.

segments_hinglish.text: Subtopic को उन mistakes के साथ बंद करता हूँ जो चुपचाप marks खाती हैं, ताकि आप इन्हें ख़ुद में पकड़ सको।

सबसे common error है AND को OR से confuse करना: mutually exclusive alternatives को multiply करना, या sequential stages को add करना। हमेशा पहले words को ANDs और ORs में translate करो, फिर ही times या plus assign करो।

दूसरी, by default no repetition मान लेना। कई students reflex में falling products लिखते हैं। पर locks, number plates, passwords आम तौर पर repetition allow करते हैं, जो n to the r है, falling product नहीं। यही fork सब तय करता है।

तीसरी, boundary constraints भूलना। Digit problems में leading digit आम तौर पर zero नहीं हो सकता, और दो exclusions एक साथ झेल सकता है, जैसे न zero न nine, जो eight options छोड़ता है, nine नहीं। सबसे constrained position पहले भरो।
चौथी, zero factorial को ग़लत handle करना। यह one है, कभी zero नहीं। इसे zero मानना आगे आने वाले combination formulas को बेकार कर देता है।
पाँचवीं, overlapping OR-cases add करना। Addition principle को cases mutually exclusive चाहिए। अगर दोनों piles में common members हैं, naive adding double गिनता है, और overlap वापस घटाना पड़ता है।
<whisper>और gold जैसा pro-tip: जब भी 'at least one' दिखे, casework में मत घिसो। Total minus none निकालो। यह messy sum को लगभग हर बार दो clean products में बदल देता है।

title: Order matters: the soul of a permutation

board_content.text: A permutation = arranging objects in a DEFINITE order.
100m podium: Ravi-Meera-Sory is a DIFFERENT result from Meera-Ravi-Sory.
The one word to tattoo on your brain: ORDER MATTERS.
Contrast: picking 3 for a study group. Ravi-Meera-Sory = Meera-Ravi-Sory. Order irrelevant.
List all orders of A, B, C: ABC, ACB, BAC, BCA, CAB, CBA. Exactly six, none repeated.
Permutation = positions. Combination = committee.

segments_english.text: In the last subtopic you learned to count outcomes. A permutation is one supremely common kind of counting: arranging objects in a definite order.

Picture the medal ceremony after a hundred metre final. If Ravi, Meera, and Sory take gold, silver, and bronze, that is a different outcome from Meera, Ravi, and Sory, even though the same three people are involved. The positions are distinguishable.
That is the soul of a permutation, and it is the one word to tattoo on your brain: order matters. Rearranging the same objects produces a brand new arrangement.

Now contrast it with picking three students to form a study group. Here Ravi, Meera, Sory is the same group as Meera, Ravi, Sory. Order is irrelevant, and that second kind of counting is a combination, which is the next subtopic.
See it with tiny numbers. List every arrangement of the three letters A, B, C taken all at a time: A B C, A C B, B A C, B C A, C A B, C B A.
That is exactly six of them, and not one is a repeat, because six is three factorial. Notice A B C and A C B are counted separately: same letters, different order, different permutation.

So carry one line into everything that follows. Permutation means positions; combination means committee. Getting that distinction firm now saves you from the single most common error in the whole chapter.

segments_hinglish.text: पिछले subtopic में आपने outcomes count करना सीखा। Permutation counting का एक बहुत common kind है: objects को एक definite order में arrange करना।
सौ metre final के बाद medal ceremony सोचो। अगर Ravi, Meera, और Sory gold, silver, bronze लेते हैं, तो यह Meera, Ravi, Sory से अलग outcome है, भले ही वही तीन log हों। Positions distinguishable हैं।
यही permutation की जान है, और यही वो एक word है दिमाग़ पर tattoo करने लायक: order matters। वही objects को rearrange करना एक बिल्कुल नया arrangement बनाता है।

अब इसे तीन students चुनकर study group बनाने से contrast करो। यहाँ Ravi, Meera, Sory वही group है जो Meera, Ravi, Sory। Order irrelevant है, और यह दूसरी तरह की counting combination है, जो अगला subtopic है।
इसे छोटे numbers से देखो। तीन letters A, B, C के सारे arrangements list करो: A B C, A C B, B A C, B C A, C A B, C B A।
ये ठीक छह हैं, और एक भी repeat नहीं, क्योंकि six is three factorial। ध्यान दो A B C और A C B अलग गिने जाते हैं: वही letters, अलग order, अलग permutation।
तो एक line आगे हर जगह ले जाओ। Permutation मतलब positions; combination मतलब committee। यह distinction अभी firm कर लेना पूरे chapter की सबसे common error से बचाता है।

title: Four flavours of permutation

board_content.text: Recognising the flavour is half the battle.
1) All distinct, no repetition (medal podium). Counted by ${}^{n}P_r$.
2) Repetition allowed (PIN, number plate). Every slot sees all n: $n^r$.
3) Some objects identical (SAMOSA). Swapping the two S's makes no new word: divide out.
4) Arranged in a circle (round table). Rotate one seat and it's the same: $(n-1)!$
Spot the flavour FIRST; the correct formula then follows.
A curved row of bolted-down chairs is still linear, not circular. Don't be fooled.

segments_english.text: Permutations come in a few important flavours, and recognising which one you are in is genuinely half the battle.
Flavour one: all objects distinct, no repetition. This is the medal podium, where each object is used at most once and every position differs. It is counted by n permute r.

Flavour two: repetition allowed, like a PIN or a number plate, where the same digit can reappear. Here every slot sees all n options afresh, giving n to the r. That is the counting principle result from the last subtopic, now living inside permutations.

Flavour three: some objects are identical, like arranging the letters of the word SAMOSA. Swapping the two S's does not create a new word, so we must divide out that redundancy, and plain n permute r no longer applies.

Flavour four: arranged in a circle, like guests around a round dining table. Rotating everyone one seat over gives the same arrangement, so the circle quietly removes one degree of freedom, and the count is n minus one factorial.
The discipline is simple. Spot the flavour first, and the correct formula follows almost automatically. Mixing up the flavour is where most marks are lost.

One honest warning: a curved row of chairs bolted to the floor is still a straight line for our purposes. It only counts as circular if rotating the whole arrangement genuinely gives the same seating.

segments_hinglish.text: Permutations कुछ important flavours में आते हैं, और आप कौन से में हो यह पहचानना सच में आधी लड़ाई है।
Flavour one: सारे objects distinct, no repetition। यह medal podium है, जहाँ हर object ज़्यादा से ज़्यादा एक बार use होता है और हर position अलग है। इसे n permute r से count करते हैं।

Flavour two: repetition allowed, जैसे PIN या number plate, जहाँ वही digit दोबारा आ सकता है। यहाँ हर slot को सारे n options फिर से दिखते हैं, यानी n to the r। यह पिछले subtopic का counting principle result है, अब permutations के अंदर।

Flavour three: कुछ objects identical, जैसे word SAMOSA के letters arrange करना। दोनों S swap करने से नया word नहीं बनता, तो हमें वो redundancy divide out करनी पड़ती है, और plain n permute r अब लागू नहीं होता।

Flavour four: circle में arrange, जैसे round dining table के guests। सबको एक seat घुमा दो तो वही arrangement मिलता है, तो circle चुपचाप एक degree of freedom हटा देता है, और count है n minus one factorial।
Discipline simple है। पहले flavour पहचानो, correct formula लगभग automatically आ जाता है। Flavour gadbad करना ही जहाँ ज़्यादातर marks जाते हैं।
एक honest warning: floor पर bolted chairs की curved row हमारे लिए अब भी straight line है। यह तभी circular गिना जाता है जब पूरे arrangement को घुमाने से सच में वही seating मिले।

title: The permutation formulas

board_content.text: Your permutation toolkit
Bridge to combinations: ${}^{n}P_r = r! \cdot {}^{n}C_r$.
Sanity: ${}^{n}P_r$ is always a positive integer; a fractional answer means you erred.

segments_english.text: Let me lay the permutation formulas on one board so you can grab the right one at a glance.
The headline: n permute r equals n times n minus one, down to n minus r plus one, which compresses to n factorial over n minus r factorial, valid for r between zero and n.
Keep the special cases handy. n permute n is n factorial, n permute zero is one, and n permute one is just n.
When repetition is allowed, drop the falling product and use n to the r, because every slot sees all n options again.
When the objects are not all distinct, with p alike of one kind, q of another, and so on, divide n factorial by p factorial, q factorial, and each look-alike group's factorial.
For a circular arrangement of all n objects the count is n minus one factorial; and if the circle can be flipped over, like a necklace or a key-ring, divide by a further two.
Store one bridge for later: n permute r equals r factorial times n choose r. Arranging equals selecting and then ordering, and this single identity ties the two halves of the chapter together.
And a sanity check to lean on: n permute r is always a positive integer for valid r. If your permutation count ever comes out as a fraction, you have made a slip somewhere.

segments_hinglish.text: Permutation formulas एक board पर रख देता हूँ ताकि सही वाला एक नज़र में पकड़ सको।
Headline: n permute r बराबर n into n minus one, नीचे n minus r plus one तक, जो compress होकर n factorial over n minus r factorial बनता है, valid r zero से n के बीच।
Special cases handy रखो। n permute n है n factorial, n permute zero है one, और n permute one बस n।
जब repetition allowed हो, falling product छोड़ो और n to the r use करो, क्योंकि हर slot को सारे n options फिर दिखते हैं।
जब objects सारे distinct न हों, p एक तरह के alike, q दूसरे, वग़ैरह, तो n factorial को p factorial, q factorial, और हर look-alike group के factorial से divide करो।
सारे n objects के circular arrangement के लिए count है n minus one factorial; और अगर circle flip हो सके, जैसे necklace या key-ring, तो और two से divide करो।
एक bridge आगे के लिए store करो: n permute r बराबर r factorial into n choose r। Arranging बराबर selecting फिर ordering, और यह एक identity chapter के दोनों हिस्सों को जोड़ती है।
और एक sanity check: n permute r valid r के लिए हमेशा positive integer होता है। अगर permutation count कभी fraction आए, कहीं slip हुआ है।

title: Deriving nPr from the counting principle

board_content.text: Why ${}^{n}P_r = \dfrac{n!}{(n-r)!}$

board_content.caption: r ordered positions, each losing one option

board_content.text: Position 1: n objects. Position 2: n-1. Position 3: n-2. ... Position r: $(n-r+1)$.
Multiply and divide by the missing tail $(n-r)! = (n-r)(n-r-1)\cdots 1$.
It's just the counting principle applied to r ordered slots.

segments_english.text: This is a board-favourite derivation, so let us build n permute r from the counting principle, step by step.
We want the number of ways to fill r ordered positions using n distinct objects, with no repetition. Treat the positions as a row of boxes.

Position one can take any of the n objects. Position two can take any object except the one already used, so n minus one. Position three has n minus two, and so on, until position r, where r minus one objects are gone, leaving n minus r plus one.
Multiplying by the counting principle gives n times n minus one, times n minus two, all the way to n minus r plus one. That falling product is the raw form of n permute r.
To compress it into a clean formula, multiply and divide by the missing tail, which is n minus r factorial, the product of everything below n minus r plus one down to one.
The numerator now runs all the way from n down to one, which is simply n factorial, over n minus r factorial. So n permute r equals n factorial over n minus r factorial.
Read what just happened: this whole result is nothing but the counting principle applied to r ordered slots, with the tail folded in to make the algebra tidy.

segments_hinglish.text: यह board का favourite derivation है, तो n permute r को counting principle से step by step बनाते हैं।
हमें चाहिए कितने तरीक़ों से r ordered positions n distinct objects से भरें, no repetition। Positions को boxes की एक row समझो।

Position one कोई भी n objects ले सकता है। Position two पहले से used को छोड़कर कोई भी, यानी n minus one। Position three के n minus two, और ऐसे ही, position r तक, जहाँ r minus one objects जा चुके, बचता है n minus r plus one।
Counting principle से multiply करने पर मिलता है n into n minus one, into n minus two, n minus r plus one तक। यह falling product ही n permute r का raw रूप है।
इसे clean formula में compress करने के लिए, missing tail से multiply और divide करो, जो है n minus r factorial, यानी n minus r plus one के नीचे से one तक सब कुछ।
अब numerator पूरा n से नीचे one तक चलता है, जो बस n factorial है, over n minus r factorial। तो n permute r बराबर n factorial over n minus r factorial।
जो हुआ उसे पढ़ो: यह पूरा result बस counting principle है जो r ordered slots पर लगा है, tail को अंदर fold करके algebra साफ़ कर दी।

title: Deriving the alike-objects and circular formulas

board_content.text: Two corrections: identical objects, and the circle
Alike: pretend the p identical objects are labelled, giving $n!$. But they permute in $p!$ invisible ways.

board_content.caption: Each circle = n linear reads, so divide n! by n

board_content.text: Circular: reading a circle from each of its n objects gives n linear arrangements, all the same circle.
Flip identical (necklace/ring)? Divide by a further 2: $\dfrac{(n-1)!}{2}$.

segments_english.text: Two of the four flavours need a correction to the plain factorial, and both come from the same idea: over-counting.

Take the alike-objects case first. Pretend, for a moment, that the p identical objects are secretly labelled, so all n are distinct. Then there are n factorial arrangements. But those labels are invisible.

The p identical objects can be shuffled among themselves in p factorial ways without changing the visible arrangement, so every real arrangement has been counted p factorial times. Divide it out, and with several repeated groups you divide by each group's factorial.
Now the circle, with a concrete check on the board: three friends X, Y, Z around a round table.

Take any one circular seating and read it off starting from each person in turn. That produces n different linear strings, yet they all describe the same circle, because rotating the table reseats no one. So each circle maps to exactly n linear arrangements.

There are n factorial linear arrangements in total, so the number of circles is n factorial over n, which is n minus one factorial. For three friends that predicts two, and indeed only two genuinely different circles exist.
One last twist: if a mirror flip counts as the same, like a necklace or a key-ring turned over, each circle is double counted, so you divide by a further two.

segments_hinglish.text: चार flavours में से दो को plain factorial में correction चाहिए, और दोनों एक ही idea से आती हैं: over-counting।
पहले alike-objects case लो। एक पल के लिए मान लो कि p identical objects secretly labelled हैं, तो सारे n distinct। तब n factorial arrangements होते हैं। पर वो labels invisible हैं।

वो p identical objects आपस में p factorial ways में shuffle हो सकते हैं बिना visible arrangement बदले, तो हर real arrangement p factorial बार गिना गया। इसे divide out करो, और कई repeated groups हों तो हर group के factorial से divide करो।
अब circle, board पर एक concrete check के साथ: तीन friends X, Y, Z round table के around।

कोई एक circular seating लो और उसे हर person से शुरू करके पढ़ो। इससे n अलग linear strings बनती हैं, फिर भी सब वही circle describe करती हैं, क्योंकि table घुमाने से कोई reseat नहीं होता। तो हर circle ठीक n linear arrangements पर map होता है।
Total n factorial linear arrangements हैं, तो circles की संख्या है n factorial over n, यानी n minus one factorial। तीन friends के लिए यह two predict करता है, और सच में सिर्फ़ दो अलग circles होते हैं।
एक last twist: अगर mirror flip को same गिना जाए, जैसे palta हुआ necklace या key-ring, तो हर circle double गिना जाता है, तो और two से divide करो।

title: Restricted permutations & the bridge to combinations

board_content.text: Three restriction reflexes

board_content.svg: <svg font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" viewBox="0 0 470 150" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><text x="10" y="18" font-size="12" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-weight="bold">TOGETHER: glue into one block</text><rect x="10" y="30" width="70" height="32" fill="#ffe8b0" stroke="#333"/><text x="28" y="51" font-size="13" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif">(A B)</text><rect x="92" y="30" width="32" height="32" fill="none" stroke="#333"/><text x="103" y="51" font-size="13" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif">C</text><rect x="128" y="30" width="32" height="32" fill="none" stroke="#333"/><text x="139" y="51" font-size="13" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif">D</text><text x="172" y="51" font-size="12" fill="#c8102e" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif">then × block's 2!</text><text x="10" y="100" font-size="12" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-weight="bold">NOT TOGETHER: fill the gaps</text><text x="10" y="128" font-size="16" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif">_ C _ D _ E _</text><text x="180" y="128" font-size="12" fill="#c8102e" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif">drop A, B into separate gaps</text></svg>
board_content.caption: Together = glue a block; not together = fill the gaps

board_content.text: TOGETHER: glue the group into one block, arrange, then $\times$ the block's internal $k!$.
A, B together among A-E: glue (AB) into 4 units. $4! \times 2! = 48$.
NOT TOGETHER: seat the others first, then drop the restricted items into the gaps.
FIXED position: lock the constrained object first, then permute the rest.

segments_english.text: Restricted permutations look scary but reduce to three reflexes. Learn them once and they cover almost every exam variant.
First reflex, must be together: glue the objects that must stay together into a single block, arrange that block among the others, then multiply by the internal arrangements of the block.

Concretely, arrange A, B, C, D, E in a row with A and B together. Glue them as one block, giving four units, arranged in four factorial, which is twenty four ways; the block itself flips in two factorial, that is two ways; so twenty four times two is forty eight.
Second reflex, must not be together: seat all the other objects first. They create gaps, including the two ends, and you drop the restricted objects into separate gaps.

For the same five letters with A and B apart, seat C, D, E first in three factorial, that is six ways, creating four gaps. Place A and B into two of those four gaps in four permute two, which is twelve. Six times twelve is seventy two. And notice forty eight plus seventy two equals one hundred twenty, which is five factorial, the total. Together and not-together must partition everything.
That partition check is the honesty test that catches errors, so use it whenever you can.
Third reflex, a fixed position: lock the constrained object in place first, then freely permute whatever remains. Constraints handled first, freedom last.
And carry forward the bridge that unifies the chapter: n permute r equals r factorial times n choose r. A permutation is simply a combination that has then been put in order.

segments_hinglish.text: Restricted permutations डरावनी लगती हैं पर तीन reflexes में सिमट जाती हैं। इन्हें एक बार सीख लो, ये लगभग हर exam variant cover करती हैं।
पहली reflex, must be together: जिन objects को साथ रहना है उन्हें एक single block में glue करो, उस block को बाकियों के बीच arrange करो, फिर block के internal arrangements से multiply करो।

Concretely, A, B, C, D, E को एक row में arrange करो with A और B together। इन्हें एक block बनाओ, तो चार units, arranged in four factorial, यानी twenty four ways; block ख़ुद two factorial में flip होता है, यानी two ways; तो twenty four into two is forty eight।
दूसरी reflex, must not be together: पहले बाकी सारे objects बिठाओ। वो gaps बनाते हैं, दोनों ends समेत, और restricted objects को अलग-अलग gaps में डालो।

उन्हीं पाँच letters के लिए A और B apart: पहले C, D, E बिठाओ three factorial में, यानी six ways, चार gaps बनते हैं। A और B को उन चार में से दो gaps में रखो four permute two में, यानी twelve। Six into twelve is seventy two। और ध्यान दो forty eight plus seventy two बराबर one hundred twenty, जो five factorial है, total। Together और not-together को सब कुछ partition करना ही है।
यह partition check honesty test है जो errors पकड़ता है, तो जब भी हो सके use करो।
तीसरी reflex, fixed position: constrained object को पहले lock करो, फिर बचा हुआ freely permute करो। Constraints पहले, freedom आख़िर में।
और chapter को जोड़ने वाला bridge आगे ले जाओ: n permute r बराबर r factorial into n choose r। Permutation बस एक combination है जिसे फिर order में रखा गया।

title: nPr in action, and the alike-objects trap

board_content.text: Example 1 (CBSE): President, Secretary, Treasurer from 8 members
Three DISTINCT posts, no one holds two, so order matters: ${}^{8}P_3$.
Example 2 (trap): arrangements of SAMOSA
6 letters: S, A, M, O, S, A. S appears twice, A appears twice.
Reflex $6! = 720$ forgets swapping identical letters makes no new word.

segments_english.text: Let us convert the theory into two clean worked examples, one straight and one a classic trap.
segments_english.tts_description: a warm 30s female hindi accent voice, conversational pacing, neutral register, elearning_instructor.

segments_english.text: Example one, CBSE level. A club has eight members, and we must fill the distinct posts of President, Secretary, and Treasurer, with no member holding two.
segments_english.tts_description: a warm 30s female hindi accent voice, conversational pacing, neutral register, elearning_instructor.

segments_english.text: Three distinct posts mean order matters, so this is eight permute three. That is eight factorial over five factorial, which is eight times seven times six, giving three hundred thirty six ways.
segments_english.tts_description: a warm 30s female hindi accent voice, conversational pacing, neutral register, elearning_instructor.

segments_english.text: Example two is a conceptual trap: count the distinct arrangements of all the letters of the word SAMOSA.
segments_english.tts_description: a warm 30s female hindi accent voice, conversational pacing, neutral register, elearning_instructor.

segments_english.text: First scan for repeats. The letters are S, A, M, O, S, A, so six letters in all, with S appearing twice and A appearing twice, while M and O appear once each.
segments_english.tts_description: a warm 30s female hindi accent voice, conversational pacing, neutral register, elearning_instructor.

segments_english.text: If all six were distinct, the answer would be six factorial, which is seven hundred twenty. But the two S's are interchangeable, so divide by two factorial, and the two A's likewise, so divide by another two factorial. Six factorial over two factorial times two factorial is seven hundred twenty over four, which is one hundred eighty.
segments_english.tts_description: a warm 30s female hindi accent voice, conversational pacing, neutral register, elearning_instructor.

segments_english.text: The trap is writing six factorial equals seven hundred twenty and stopping, forgetting that swapping the identical letters produces no new word. Always scan for repeats before reaching for a factorial.
segments_english.tts_description: a warm 30s female hindi accent voice, conversational pacing, neutral register, elearning_instructor.

segments_hinglish.text: Theory को दो clean worked examples में बदलते हैं, एक straight और एक classic trap।
segments_hinglish.tts_description: a warm 30s female hindi accent voice, conversational pacing, neutral register, elearning_instructor.

segments_hinglish.text: Example one, CBSE level। एक club में आठ members हैं, और हमें distinct posts President, Secretary, Treasurer भरने हैं, कोई member दो न रखे।
segments_hinglish.tts_description: a warm 30s female hindi accent voice, conversational pacing, neutral register, elearning_instructor.

segments_hinglish.text: तीन distinct posts मतलब order matters, तो यह eight permute three है। यानी eight factorial over five factorial, जो है eight into seven into six, यानी three hundred thirty six ways।
segments_hinglish.tts_description: a warm 30s female hindi accent voice, conversational pacing, neutral register, elearning_instructor.

segments_hinglish.text: Example two एक conceptual trap है: word SAMOSA के सारे letters के distinct arrangements गिनो।
segments_hinglish.tts_description: a warm 30s female hindi accent voice, conversational pacing, neutral register, elearning_instructor.

segments_hinglish.text: पहले repeats scan करो। Letters हैं S, A, M, O, S, A, तो कुल छह letters, S दो बार और A दो बार, जबकि M और O एक-एक बार।
segments_hinglish.tts_description: a warm 30s female hindi accent voice, conversational pacing, neutral register, elearning_instructor.

segments_hinglish.text: अगर सारे छह distinct होते, answer six factorial, यानी seven hundred twenty होता। पर दोनों S interchangeable हैं, तो two factorial से divide, और दोनों A भी, तो एक और two factorial से divide। Six factorial over two factorial into two factorial is seven hundred twenty over four, यानी one hundred eighty।
segments_hinglish.tts_description: a warm 30s female hindi accent voice, conversational pacing, neutral register, elearning_instructor.

segments_hinglish.text: Trap है six factorial equals seven hundred twenty लिखकर रुक जाना, यह भूलकर कि identical letters swap करने से नया word नहीं बनता। Factorial की तरफ़ हाथ बढ़ाने से पहले हमेशा repeats scan करो।
segments_hinglish.tts_description: a warm 30s female hindi accent voice, conversational pacing, neutral register, elearning_instructor.

title: A parity constraint, and the circular gap method

board_content.text: Example 3 (JEE Main): 4-digit even numbers from 1,2,3,4,5, no repetition
'Even' pins the units place, so handle it first. Units $\in \{2, 4\}$: 2 ways.
Example 4 (JEE Adv): 5 boys, 3 girls, round table, no two girls adjacent

board_content.caption: Seat boys first; girls go into the gaps between them

board_content.text: Seat boys first (circular): $(5-1)! = 24$. Five boys create 5 gaps.
Anchor the UNCONSTRAINED group first: the circular gap method.

segments_english.text: Two more examples, both stitching a constraint onto a permutation. The reflex, as always, is to handle the most constrained slot first.
Example three, JEE Main. Using the digits one to five without repetition, how many four-digit even numbers can we form? The word even pins down the units place, so we settle that first.

The units digit must be even, so it comes from the set two, four, giving two choices. The remaining three positions are filled from the four unused digits with order mattering, which is four permute three, equal to twenty four.
Multiply: two times twenty four is forty eight even four-digit numbers. The parity restriction fixed one slot, and n permute r arranged the rest.
Example four is a lovely JEE Advanced one: seat five boys and three girls around a circular table so that no two girls sit next to each other.

Build it in the order that respects the constraint. Seat the boys first, and since it is circular, that is five minus one factorial, which is twenty four. The five seated boys create five gaps between them.

To keep the girls apart, each girl goes into a separate gap. Choosing and ordering three girls into five gaps is five permute three, equal to sixty. So the total is twenty four times sixty, which is one thousand four hundred forty.

The rigorous move is anchoring the unconstrained group first. Seating the girls directly would tangle the no-adjacency condition into the circular count; seating boys first turns the restriction into a clean gap-filling step. That is the circular gap method.

segments_hinglish.text: दो और examples, दोनों एक constraint को permutation पर stitch करते हैं। Reflex, हमेशा की तरह, सबसे constrained slot पहले handle करना।
Example three, JEE Main। Digits one से five बिना repetition use करके, कितने four-digit even numbers बना सकते हैं? Word even units place को pin करता है, तो पहले उसे settle करो।
Units digit even होना चाहिए, तो यह set two, four से आता है, यानी two choices। बाकी तीन positions चार unused digits से भरते हैं order मायने रखते हुए, जो four permute three है, बराबर twenty four।
Multiply: two into twenty four is forty eight even four-digit numbers। Parity restriction ने एक slot fix किया, और n permute r ने बाकी arrange किए।
Example four एक सुंदर JEE Advanced है: पाँच boys और तीन girls को round table के around बिठाओ ताकि कोई दो girls साथ न बैठें।
इसे उस order में बनाओ जो constraint का सम्मान करे। पहले boys बिठाओ, और चूँकि circular है, यह five minus one factorial है, यानी twenty four। पाँच बैठे boys उनके बीच पाँच gaps बनाते हैं।

Girls को अलग रखने के लिए, हर girl एक अलग gap में जाती है। तीन girls को पाँच gaps में choose और order करना five permute three है, बराबर sixty। तो total है twenty four into sixty, यानी one thousand four hundred forty।

Rigorous move है unconstrained group को पहले anchor करना। Girls को सीधे बिठाना no-adjacency condition को circular count में उलझा देता। Boys पहले बिठाने से restriction एक clean gap-filling step बन जाती है। यही circular gap method है।

title: Pitfalls & pro-tips for permutations

board_content.text: Where permutation marks leak away
Order confusion: using ${}^{n}P_r$ when order doesn't matter. Test: swap two chosen, new outcome?
Forgetting to divide for alike objects: writing $n!$ for a word with repeated letters.
Circular slips: $n!$ instead of $(n-1)!$, or forgetting $\div 2$ for necklaces/rings.
Repetition fork: defaulting to ${}^{n}P_r$ when repetition is allowed (that's $n^r$).
Restrictions: together $\to$ block ($\times$ internal); not together $\to$ gap method.
On a circle, fix one object to kill rotation; it collapses to a linear problem.

segments_english.text: Let me close permutations with the mistakes that quietly leak marks, so you can catch them in your own working.

The big one is order confusion: using n permute r when order does not actually matter, where you really wanted n choose r. Always run the master test. If you swap two chosen objects, is it a new outcome? Yes means permutation; no means combination.
Second, forgetting to divide for alike objects, that is writing n factorial for a word with repeated letters. Always scan for repeats and quotient them out.

Third, circular slips. Using n factorial instead of n minus one factorial for a round arrangement, or forgetting the extra divide by two for necklaces, bracelets, and key-rings that can be flipped over.
Fourth, the repetition fork. Defaulting to n permute r when the problem actually allows repetition. That case is n to the r, not a falling product.

For restrictions, keep the two reflexes crisp. For together, glue the group into one block, arrange, then multiply by the block's internal arrangements. For not together, seat everyone else first and drop the restricted items into the gaps.
<whisper>And the one that saves the most time on a circle: fix one object to kill the rotational symmetry, and the whole problem collapses to a familiar linear one on the remaining objects.

segments_hinglish.text: Permutations को उन mistakes के साथ बंद करता हूँ जो चुपचाप marks leak करती हैं, ताकि आप अपनी working में इन्हें पकड़ सको।

बड़ी वाली है order confusion: n permute r use करना जब order सच में मायने नहीं रखता, जहाँ आपको असल में n choose r चाहिए था। हमेशा master test चलाओ। अगर दो chosen objects swap करो, क्या नया outcome है? हाँ मतलब permutation; नहीं मतलब combination।
दूसरी, alike objects के लिए divide करना भूलना, यानी repeated letters वाले word के लिए n factorial लिखना। हमेशा repeats scan करो और quotient out करो।
तीसरी, circular slips। Round arrangement के लिए n minus one factorial की जगह n factorial, या flip हो सकने वाले necklaces, bracelets, key-rings के लिए extra divide by two भूलना।
चौथी, repetition fork। n permute r पर default करना जब problem असल में repetition allow करता है। वो case n to the r है, falling product नहीं।

Restrictions के लिए दोनों reflexes crisp रखो। Together के लिए group को एक block में glue करो, arrange करो, फिर block के internal arrangements से multiply करो। Not together के लिए पहले बाकी सबको बिठाओ और restricted items को gaps में डालो।
<whisper>और circle पर सबसे ज़्यादा time बचाने वाली: एक object fix करके rotational symmetry ख़त्म करो, और पूरा problem बचे objects पर एक familiar linear problem में collapse हो जाता है।

title: Order doesn't matter: the combination

board_content.text: A combination = SELECT a group; order is irrelevant.
Cricket selectors pick 11 from 16. Same team however the names were listed.
The watchword flips: ORDER DOESN'T MATTER.

board_content.text: Handshakes among 9 people are pairs, order-free: ${}^{9}C_2 = 36$, not ${}^{9}P_2 = 72$.
A combination is a permutation with the ordering stripped: divide ${}^{n}P_r$ by $r!$.
Selection alone $\to$ combination. Selection + roles $\to$ permutation.

segments_english.text: In the last subtopic order was everything. A combination is the mirror image: you only select a group of objects, and order is completely irrelevant.

Picture the selectors of a cricket squad choosing eleven players from a pool of sixteen. Once the eleven names are down, it makes no difference whether a selector wrote them top to bottom or in any other sequence. The team is the same set of eleven people.
So the watchword flips. In permutations it was order matters; in combinations it is order does not matter. If you shuffle the chosen objects and get nothing new, you are looking at a combination.
See it with pairs on the board. From four objects A, B, C, D the selections of size two are A B, A C, A D, B C, B D, C D, exactly six of them, because A B and B A are the same pair, not two.

This is why handshakes among nine people number nine choose two, which is thirty six, and not nine permute two, which is seventy two. A shakes with B and B shakes with A are the same handshake, so we strip that order away.

That gives the whole idea in one line: a combination is a permutation with the ordering stripped off. You take n permute r and divide by r factorial, the number of ways the chosen group could be reordered.
So keep the test sharp. Selection alone is a combination. Selection plus roles, ranks, or positions is a permutation, and it costs you the extra r factorial.

segments_hinglish.text: पिछले subtopic में order ही सब कुछ था। Combination उसका mirror image है: आप बस objects का एक group select करते हो, और order पूरी तरह irrelevant है।

एक cricket squad के selectors सोचो जो sixteen के pool में से eleven players चुनते हैं। जब eleven names लिख गए, फ़र्क़ नहीं पड़ता selector ने उन्हें ऊपर से नीचे लिखा या किसी और sequence में। Team वही eleven log का set है।
तो watchword flip हो जाता है। Permutations में था order matters; combinations में है order does not matter। अगर chosen objects shuffle करने पर कुछ नया न मिले, तो आप combination देख रहे हो।
इसे board पर pairs से देखो। चार objects A, B, C, D से size two की selections हैं A B, A C, A D, B C, B D, C D, ठीक छह, क्योंकि A B और B A वही pair है, दो नहीं।

इसीलिए nine people के बीच handshakes की संख्या nine choose two है, यानी thirty six, न कि nine permute two, यानी seventy two। A का B से shake और B का A से shake वही handshake है, तो हम वो order strip कर देते हैं।
यह पूरा idea एक line में दे देता है: combination एक permutation है जिससे ordering strip कर दी गई। आप n permute r लेते हो और r factorial से divide करते हो, यानी chosen group को reorder करने के तरीक़े।
तो test तेज़ रखो। सिर्फ़ selection combination है। Selection plus roles, ranks, या positions permutation है, और यह आपको extra r factorial का ख़र्च देता है।

title: The combination formula and its properties

board_content.text: Your combination toolkit

board_content.latex: \text{if } {}^{n}C_{r} = {}^{n}C_{s}: \; r = s \text{ or } r + s = n

board_content.text: Symmetry shortcut: ${}^{12}C_{10} = {}^{12}C_2 = 66$; never grind the big factorial.

segments_english.text: Let me put the combination formulas on one board. They are all examinable, so learn to read them fluently.
The core: n choose r equals n factorial over r factorial times n minus r factorial, which also equals n permute r divided by r factorial, valid for r between zero and n.
The boundaries: n choose zero and n choose n are both one, n choose one is n, and n choose r is zero whenever r exceeds n, since you cannot choose more objects than exist.
The symmetry property, and it is the most useful one: n choose r equals n choose n minus r. Choosing which r to keep is the same act as choosing which n minus r to reject.
Pascal's rule: n choose r plus n choose r minus one equals n plus one choose r. We will prove this by a single yes or no question in a moment.
And one more identity: if n choose r equals n choose s, then either r equals s, or r plus s equals n. That second possibility is easy to forget and examiners love it.
Lean on symmetry to save arithmetic. To compute twelve choose ten, rewrite it as twelve choose two, which is sixty six. Never grind through the large factorial when the small twin is right there.

segments_hinglish.text: Combination formulas एक board पर रख देता हूँ। ये सब examinable हैं, तो इन्हें fluently पढ़ना सीखो।
Core: n choose r बराबर n factorial over r factorial into n minus r factorial, जो n permute r divided by r factorial के भी बराबर है, valid r zero से n के बीच।
Boundaries: n choose zero और n choose n दोनों one, n choose one है n, और n choose r zero है जब भी r, n से ज़्यादा हो, क्योंकि मौजूद से ज़्यादा objects नहीं चुन सकते।
Symmetry property, और यही सबसे useful है: n choose r बराबर n choose n minus r। कौन से r रखने हैं यह चुनना वही act है जो कौन से n minus r reject करने हैं।
Pascal's rule: n choose r plus n choose r minus one बराबर n plus one choose r। इसे हम अभी एक yes या no सवाल से prove करेंगे।
और एक identity: अगर n choose r बराबर n choose s, तो या तो r बराबर s, या r plus s बराबर n। यह दूसरी possibility भूलना आसान है और examiners इसे पसंद करते हैं।
Arithmetic बचाने के लिए symmetry पर टिको। Twelve choose ten निकालने के लिए, इसे twelve choose two लिखो, जो है sixty six। जब छोटा twin सामने हो तो बड़े factorial में मत घिसो।

title: Deriving nCr and the symmetry property

board_content.text: Why ${}^{n}C_r = \dfrac{n!}{r!\,(n-r)!}$
Reuse the bridge: to arrange r of n, first SELECT (${}^{n}C_r$) then ORDER ($r!$).
Symmetry: choosing to keep = choosing to reject
Every group of r kept leaves a group of $n-r$ rejected. Two names for one act.

segments_english.text: The combination formula almost falls out for free once you reuse the bridge we built in permutations, so let us do exactly that.
To arrange r objects out of n in order is a two-stage job. First select which r objects to use, which is n choose r ways, then order those chosen r among themselves, which is r factorial ways.
By the counting principle, n permute r equals n choose r times r factorial.

Solve for n choose r: it is n permute r over r factorial. Substituting n permute r as n factorial over n minus r factorial gives n choose r equals n factorial over r factorial times n minus r factorial. The whole combination formula is just the permutation formula with the internal orderings divided out.
Now the symmetry property, with the elegant proof rather than the algebra.

Every time you choose a group of r objects to keep, you simultaneously leave behind a group of n minus r objects. Choosing the keepers and choosing the rejects are two descriptions of the very same act, so the two counts must be equal.
Hence n choose r equals n choose n minus r. For a quick numeric feel, seven choose five equals seven choose two, which is twenty one. Choosing five to keep is the same as choosing two to leave out.

segments_hinglish.text: Combination formula लगभग free में निकल आता है जब आप permutations में बनाया bridge reuse करते हो, तो बिल्कुल वही करते हैं।
r objects को n में से order में arrange करना two-stage job है। पहले select करो कौन से r use करने हैं, यानी n choose r ways, फिर उन chosen r को आपस में order करो, यानी r factorial ways।
Counting principle से, n permute r बराबर n choose r into r factorial।

n choose r के लिए solve करो: यह n permute r over r factorial है। n permute r को n factorial over n minus r factorial रखने पर मिलता है n choose r बराबर n factorial over r factorial into n minus r factorial। पूरा combination formula बस permutation formula है जिससे internal orderings divide कर दी गईं।
अब symmetry property, algebra की जगह elegant proof के साथ।
हर बार जब आप r objects रखने के लिए चुनते हो, आप साथ ही n minus r objects पीछे छोड़ देते हो। Keepers चुनना और rejects चुनना उसी एक act के दो descriptions हैं, तो दोनों counts बराबर होने चाहिए।
इसलिए n choose r बराबर n choose n minus r। एक quick numeric feel के लिए, seven choose five बराबर seven choose two, यानी twenty one। पाँच रखने के लिए चुनना वही है जो दो छोड़ने के लिए चुनना।

title: Pascal's rule and selection under constraints

board_content.text: Pascal's rule by one yes/no question
